'''Keith Alexander Nugent''' {{post-nominals|country=AUS|AO}} [[Australian Academy of Science|FAA]] (born 28 June 1959{{cn|date=September 2025}}) is an Australian physicist.<ref name="Trove">{{cite web|title=Nugent, Keith Alexander (1959-)|url=http://nla.gov.au/nla.party-1476370|access-date=11 May 2012|work=Trove|publisher=National Library of Australia}}</ref> He is Emeritus Professor of Physics at the [[Australian National University]] (ANU) in [[Canberra]].

He was the Deputy Vice-Chancellor (Research and Innovation) of the Australian National University (ANU) from January 2019 to January 2024. 

Prior to this he was Deputy Vice-Chancellor and Vice-President (Research) at [[La Trobe University]],<ref>{{Cite web|title=Keith Nugent at La Trobe|url=https://scholars.latrobe.edu.au/knugent|access-date=2021-12-17|website=scholars.latrobe.edu.au}}</ref> [[Victoria (Australia)|Victoria]], and a Laureate Professor of [[Physics]] at the [[University of Melbourne]], specialising in [[X-ray optics]] and [[Atomic, molecular, and optical physics#Optical physics|optical physics]].

He received a first-class honours degree from the [[University of Adelaide]]<ref name="bv">{{cite web|url=http://www.business.vic.gov.au/BUSVIC/STANDARD/1001/PC_60664.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070325233613/http://www.business.vic.gov.au/BUSVIC/STANDARD/1001/PC_60664.html|archive-date=2007-03-25|title=Professor Keith Nugent |last=|first=|date=2007-03-25|website=Business Victoria}}</ref> and his [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] from the [[Australian National University|ANU]]. Nugent is a Fellow of the [[Australian Academy of Science National Committees|Australian Academy of Science]] (FAA),<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Keith Nugent|url=https://www.science.org.au/profile/keith-nugent|access-date=2021-12-17|website=www.science.org.au|language=en}}</ref> and is known for his research in X-ray optics, X-ray free electron laser science, novel approaches to microscopy and [[Phase-contrast X-ray imaging|X-ray phase contrast imaging]].

== Early life and education ==
{{unreferencedsect|date=August 2025}}
Nugent was born in [[Bath, Somerset|Bath]], [[England]], where his father was a chocolate chemist for [[J. S. Fry & Sons|Fry & Sons]]. The family, including Nugent’s mother and his two brothers, moved to Australia when he was 11, when his father took up a role at Red Tulip (since taken over by [[Cadbury]]) in [[Melbourne]]. The family moved again to country NSW and Nugent completed his schooling at [[Batlow, New South Wales|Batlow]] Central School.

He undertook a BSc in [[Physics]] and [[Theoretical physics|Theoretical Physics]] at [[Australian National University|ANU]], Honours in [[Physics]] at [[University of Adelaide]], then returned to the ANU to undertake a PhD in [[Laser science|Laser Physics]].

== Research and career ==

Nugent was appointed Professor at the [[University of Melbourne]] when he was 34, was elected to the [[Australian Academy of Science]] at 41 and was twice honoured as an [[Australian Research Council]] (ARC) Federation Fellow (2001 and 2006).<ref>{{Cite web|date=2006-09-07|title=Australian Synchrotron - June 2006: Lightspeed|url=http://www.synchrotron.vic.gov.au/content.asp?Document_ID=4524 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060907174739/http://www.synchrotron.vic.gov.au/content.asp?Document_ID=4524 |archive-date=2006-09-07 |access-date=2021-12-17}}</ref>

In 1989, Nugent collaborated with physicist [[Stephen W. Wilkins]] to develop a form of [[X-ray optics]] known as lobster-eye optics. Initially unknown to Wilkins and Nugent, the lobster-eye X-ray optics principle was first proposed for X-rays in the 1970s by [[Roger Angel]]. Nugent and Wilkins' key contribution was to open up an approach to manufacturing these devices using microchannel plate technology. The lobster-eye approach opened the way for X-ray telescopes with a 360 degree view of the sky. "The reason it's got such a high profile is that other X-ray telescopes see a tiny, tiny part of the sky. Although normal telescopes see a small part of the sky, X-ray telescopes see an even smaller part. The beauty (of the new telescope) is that it actually expands that field of view hundreds of times," Nugent said.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2004-08-19|title=Scientist has an all-seeing eye on the future|url=https://www.theage.com.au/national/scientist-has-an-all-seeing-eye-on-the-future-20040819-gdyhdr.html|access-date=2021-12-17|website=The Age|language=en}}</ref>

A lobster-eye X-ray satellite was successfully launched on 25 July 2020 from the [[Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center]]. The lobster-eye X-ray satellite will be the world's first in-orbit space exploration satellite equipped with such imaging technology.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Kong|first=The University of Hong|title=Launch of the world's first soft X-ray satellite with 'Lobster-Eye' imaging technology|url=https://phys.org/news/2020-07-world-soft-x-ray-satellite-lobster-eye.html|access-date=2021-12-17|website=phys.org|language=en}}</ref>

Nugent became interested in how to measure optical phase without using interferometry. This has led to new approaches to [[radiography]], electron and optical microscopy. He was the founding researcher of microscopy company IATIA,<ref>{{Cite web|title=How Iatia changed its fortunes by changing its business model|url=http://labonline.com.au/content/life-scientist/article/how-iatia-changed-its-fortunes-by-changing-its-business-model-410742326|access-date=2021-12-17|website=labonline.com.au|language=en}}</ref> created to commercialise the work of himself and his two former PhD students, David Paganin and Anton Barty, in [[Quantitative phase-contrast microscopy|quantitative phase imaging]] (QPI). IATIA’s QPI technology was able to extract phase and wavefront information from light and other wave-like radiations using conventional imaging technology, such as standard digital cameras, without the need for special optical components. From 2005, Nugent was a Member of the Board of Directors and Chair of IATIA’s Audit Committee. The company traded for 10 years but failed in 2010 due to the [[2008 financial crisis]]. IATIA was awarded the 2006 Australian Technology Showcase Patrons Award.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Iatia Imaging|url=http://iatia-imaging.com/About-us.php|access-date=2021-12-17|website=iatia-imaging.com}}</ref>

When Nugent's wife Dr Eroia Barone-Nugent developed and instigated the Growing Tall Poppies Program (2008) to increase and sustain girls in science beyond year 10 Nugent quickly included and this program in his scientific endeavors. With a focus on supporting young Australians in science his wife Dr Eroia Barone-Nugent was pivotal in showing how science centers of excellence could work with schools and curriculum to deliver on their outreach responsibilities Growing Tall Poppies Program (GTP)<ref>{{Cite web|date=2015-05-18|title=Growing Tall Poppies {{!}} MaterChristi|url=http://www.materchristi.edu.au/news/growing-tall-poppies/|access-date=2021-12-17|archive-date=18 May 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150518100713/http://www.materchristi.edu.au/news/growing-tall-poppies/|url-status=bot: unknown}}</ref> in 2008. The purpose of the student-scientist partnership program is to highlight the role of physics in solving real-world issues, and to help students become “tall poppies” in science.{{cn|date=September 2025}}

Nugent was appointed part-time director of the [[Australian Synchrotron]] from 2011-12. He had previously served as a member of its national scientific advisory board and its board of directors.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2006-09-18|title=ASSN: Profile|url=http://www.chemistry.unimelb.edu.au/staff/quiney/www/synchnet/people/nugent.php |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060918190033/http://www.chemistry.unimelb.edu.au/staff/quiney/www/synchnet/people/nugent.php |archive-date=2006-09-18 |access-date=2021-12-17}}</ref>

From 2005-2012, Nugent was director of the [[Australian Research Council|ARC]] [https://physics.unimelb.edu.au/Research/Associated-Groups-Networks/the-arc-centre-of-excellence-for-coherent-x-ray-science-cxs Centre of Excellence for Coherent X-ray Science],<ref>{{Cite web|last=Hunt|first=Catherine|date=2019-09-19|title=The ARC Centre of Excellence for Coherent X-ray Science (CXS)|url=https://physics.unimelb.edu.au/Research/Associated-Groups-Networks/the-arc-centre-of-excellence-for-coherent-x-ray-science-cxs|access-date=2021-12-17|website=School of Physics|language=en}}</ref> based at the [[University of Melbourne]], where he drove the development of coherent X-ray diffraction methods for imaging biological structures using [[Free-electron laser|X-ray free-electron lasers]].{{cn|date=September 2025}}

He was Deputy Vice-Chancellor and Vice-President (research) at [[La Trobe University]] from January 2013 to December 2018.<ref>{{Cite web|title=New appointment for La Trobe|url=http://www.latrobe.edu.au/news/articles/2012/article/new-appointment-for-la-trobe|access-date=30 August 2013|archive-date=23 January 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130123160239/http://www.latrobe.edu.au/news/articles/2012/article/new-appointment-for-la-trobe|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Nugent has been a member of the [[Australian Research Council|ARC]] Expert Advisory Committee for Physics, Chemistry and Geosciences, and the international scientific advisory board of [[Elettra Sincrotrone Trieste|Elettra Sincotrone Trieste]], the [https://www.nsrrc.org.tw/english/index.aspx National Synchrotron Radiation Research Centre] in [[Taiwan]], and the [[European XFEL|European X-ray Free Electron Laser]] based in [[Hamburg]]. He was a chief investigator for the [https://imagingcoe.org ARC Centre for Advanced Molecular Imaging].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Prof Keith Nugent – Imaging CoE|url=https://imagingcoe.org/team/prof-keith-nugent/|access-date=2021-12-17|language=en-AU}}</ref>

He is also a board member at [[National Computational Infrastructure]], the [https://www.science.org.au/about-us/governance/committees-council/governance-committees-council/committee-advisory-committee Advisory Committee on Policy Matters], [[Australian Academy of Science]] and the [https://ncig.anu.edu.au National Centre for Indigenous Genomics].

== ANU Deputy Vice-Chancellor (Research and Innovation) ==

Nugent was appointed Deputy Vice-Chancellor (Research and Innovation)<ref>{{Cite web|date=2014-10-11|title=Professor Keith Nugent|url=https://www.anu.edu.au/about/university-executive/professor-keith-nugent|access-date=2021-12-17|website=ANU|language=en}}</ref> of the [[Australian National University]] in 2019 and remained in the role until January 2024. ANU [[Provost (education)|provost]], Professor Mike Calford, said, "We sought to fill this critical role with a person who could continue to build the profile of ANU as a world-leading institution for research and development and one who understands the complex systems that support successful research".<ref>{{Cite web|date=2018-09-05|title=ANU appoints new Executive member|url=https://www.anu.edu.au/news/all-news/anu-appoints-new-executive-member|access-date=2021-12-17|website=ANU|language=en}}</ref>

== Commercial connections ==
Nugent is the non-executive director of Significant Early Venture Capital and WearOptimo. He is also the alternate director for VC at ANU Connect Ventures {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211217071132/https://www.anuconnectventures.com.au/ |date=17 December 2021 }}, and director<ref>{{Cite web|title=Deputy Vice-Chancellor ANU Research - Keith Nugent|url=https://anuenterprise.com.au/deputy-vice-chancellor-keith-nugent/|access-date=2021-12-17|website=ANU Enterprise|language=en-AU}}</ref> at [https://anuenterprise.com.au ANU Enterprise].

== Personal life ==
{{unreferencedsect|date=August 2025}}
Nugent met his wife Dr Eroia Barone-Nugent at the [[Australian National University]] in 1981. The couple have three grown-up children: two sons who live in the [[United States|USA]], and one daughter who lives in [[Australia]].

* 2016 Lloyd Rees Lecture,<ref>{{Cite web|title=XFELS focus of Lloyd Rees Lecture {{!}} Australian Academy of Science|url=https://www.science.org.au/academy-newsletter/dec-2016-106/xfels-focus-lloyd-rees-lecture|access-date=2021-12-20|website=www.science.org.au|language=en}}</ref> [[Australian Academy of Science]].
* 2011 Elected Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=APS Fellow Archive|url=http://aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm|access-date=2021-12-20|website=aps.org|language=en}}</ref>
* 2009 Victorian State Impact Grant, Schools First Award, with Dr Eroia Barone-Nugent, for the Growing Tall Poppies program.
* 2004 [https://business.vic.gov.au/grants-and-programs/victoria-prize-for-science-and-innovation Victoria Prize] for pioneering work with quantitative phase imaging.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2007-09-30|title=Media Release: PHYSICIST WINS VICTORIA'S TOP SCIENCE PRIZE|url=http://www.dpc.vic.gov.au/domino/Web_Notes/newmedia.nsf/b0222c68d27626e2ca256c8c001a3d2d/9f8eee1787665b62ca256ef4008165f6!OpenDocument |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070930223234/http://www.dpc.vic.gov.au/domino/Web_Notes/newmedia.nsf/b0222c68d27626e2ca256c8c001a3d2d/9f8eee1787665b62ca256ef4008165f6!OpenDocument |archive-date=2007-09-30 |access-date=2021-12-17}}</ref>
* 2003 [[Centenary Medal]] by the Federal Government for outstanding contributions to science.
* 2002 [https://rd100awards.com R&D 100 Award] for the development of quantitative phase microscopy.
* 2000 Elected a Fellow of the [[Australian Academy of Science]] in 2000.<ref name=":0" />
* 1997 The [[Walter Boas Medal]] (1997)<ref>{{Cite web|title=1997 Boas Medal Presentation and Lecture|url=http://vic.aip.org.au/program/1997/november.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060922200601/http://vic.aip.org.au/program/1997/november.html |archive-date=2006-09-22 |access-date=2021-12-17}}</ref> of the [[Australian Institute of Physics]], shared with Dr [[Stephen W. Wilkins]].<ref>{{Cite web|date=2012-03-17|title=Australian Institute of Physics|url=http://www.aip.org.au/content/boas |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120317120246/http://www.aip.org.au/content/boas |archive-date=2012-03-17 |access-date=2021-12-17}}</ref>

* 1989 [[Pawsey Medal]]<ref>{{Cite web|title=Pawsey Medal|url=http://www.scientificlib.com/en/Physics/Info/PawseyMedal.html|access-date=2021-12-17|website=www.scientificlib.com}}</ref> of the [[Australian Academy of Science]].
* 1988 [https://rd100awards.com R&D 100 Award] for the development of the penumbral neutron imaging camera.
